lead: A reaction can be thermodynamically possible and still stop far from complete conversion. At the current temperature, pressure and composition, compare the reaction quotient Q with the equilibrium constant K. The sign of ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) gives the spontaneous direction. Equilibrium conversion and yield then measure how far a given feed can go when Q reaches K. Engineers use this check to screen routes, size reactors and read plant data for ammonia, methanol and steam reforming.
prereq: You need: extent of reaction from 7.1, the equilibrium criterion from 7.2, K from 7.3 and composition from 7.5.

blocks.text: A reacting mixture has a composition at every instant, and that composition fixes Q. Q is not the equilibrium constant. Q changes as the reaction proceeds; K changes only with temperature.

blocks.where: aᵢ is the activity of species i relative to its standard state; νᵢ is its stoichiometric number, positive for products and negative for reactants; Π means product over all species. Activities are dimensionless, so Q is dimensionless.

blocks.text: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K)
blocks.where: ΔG is the Gibbs energy change at the current composition, J per mole of reaction as written; ΔG° is the standard Gibbs energy change, J/mol; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is absolute temperature in K; Q and K are dimensionless.

items: Q < K gives ΔG < 0: forward reaction is spontaneous.
Q = K gives ΔG = 0: the mixture is at equilibrium.
Q > K gives ΔG > 0: backward reaction is spontaneous.

blocks.text: Feasibility here means direction from the present state. K > 1 only says standard-state products are favoured. It does not fix conversion: feed composition, stoichiometry, pressure and inerts enter through Q. Pressure and inert effects are in 7.7.
For one reaction, write every mole number in terms of one extent ξ (mol). Set Q(ξ) = K and solve for ξ. Then convert extent to conversion.

blocks.where: X is the conversion of limiting reactant i, dimensionless and often reported as %; n<sub>i0</sub> is its initial moles; n<sub>i</sub> is its moles at the chosen state. At equilibrium, X<sub>eq</sub> uses n<sub>i</sub> at equilibrium.

blocks.text: For ideal gases, aᵢ = yᵢ P/P°, where yᵢ is mole fraction, P is total pressure and P° is standard pressure, 1 bar.

items: Choose a basis, usually 1 mol of limiting reactant fed.
Write nᵢ(ξ) = n<sub>i0</sub> + νᵢξ from the stoichiometric table.
Write total moles n<sub>T</sub>(ξ) and yᵢ = nᵢ/n<sub>T</sub>.
Substitute activities into Q = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>.
Set Q(ξ) = K and solve for ξ, then X<sub>eq</sub>.

blocks.text: For A ⇌ 2B with 1 mol A fed, no B and P = 1 bar: n<sub>A</sub> = 1 − ξ, n<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ, n<sub>T</sub> = 1 + ξ, so Q = 4ξ²/(1 − ξ²). The worked example solves this with K = 0.222.
Conversion tells how much limiting reactant disappeared. Yield tells how much desired product appeared. Selectivity compares desired product with undesired product.

blocks.where: Y<sub>D</sub> is yield of desired product D, dimensionless or mol D per mol limiting reactant fed; n<sub>D,formed</sub> is moles of D formed; n<sub>L0</sub> is moles of limiting reactant fed. Some texts divide by ν<sub>D</sub> n<sub>L0</sub>, where ν<sub>D</sub> is the stoichiometric number of D in the reaction as written, and call the result the fractional yield (fraction of the theoretical maximum amount of D).
S<sub>D/U</sub> is selectivity of desired product D over undesired product U, mol/mol; n<sub>U,formed</sub> is moles of U formed. Name the undesired product when several exist.

blocks.text: High selectivity does not mean high yield. A reactor may make almost pure D but convert very little feed. For several simultaneous reactions, see 7.8.

figure.caption: The same A ⇌ 2B feed at 400 K: Q = 0.0404 at ξ = 0.10 drives the reaction forward, Q = 0.396 at ξ = 0.30 drives it backward, and Q = K at ξ = 0.2293 gives equilibrium conversion 0.229.

spec.title: Q compared with K
spec.aria: A decision flow: compute Q from feed and conditions, compare with K, then choose forward, equilibrium or backward; the equilibrium branch gives extent 0.2293 mol and conversion 0.229.

examples.question: For A ⇌ 2B, K = 0.222 at 400 K. A feed of 1 mol A at 1 bar contains no B. Take ideal gas behaviour and standard pressure 1 bar. (a) Derive Q as a function of extent ξ. (b) Compute Q at ξ = 0.10 mol and ξ = 0.30 mol; state the spontaneous direction. (c) Find equilibrium extent, conversion of A and yield of B.
steps: Stoichiometric table: n<sub>A</sub> = 1 − ξ mol, n<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ mol, total n<sub>T</sub> = 1 + ξ mol.
Mole fractions: y<sub>A</sub> = (1 − ξ)/(1 + ξ), y<sub>B</sub> = 2ξ/(1 + ξ).
At P = 1 bar and P° = 1 bar, ideal-gas activities are a<sub>A</sub> = y<sub>A</sub> and a<sub>B</sub> = y<sub>B</sub>.
At ξ = 0.10 mol: Q = 4(0.10)²/(1 − 0.10²) = 0.0404. This is below K = 0.222, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction goes forward.
At ξ = 0.30 mol: Q = 4(0.30)²/(1 − 0.30²) = 0.3956 ≈ 0.396. This is above K, so ΔG > 0 and the reaction goes backward.
At equilibrium: 4ξ²/(1 − ξ²) = 0.222, so 4ξ² = 0.222 − 0.222ξ², giving 4.222ξ² = 0.222 and ξ² = 0.05258.
ξ<sub>eq</sub> = 0.2293 mol. Conversion of A: X = ξ/1 = 0.2293, or 22.9%.
Yield of B: n<sub>B,formed</sub>/n<sub>A0</sub> = 2ξ/1 = 0.4586 ≈ 0.459 mol B per mol A fed.
examples.answer: Q(0.10) = 0.0404 < K, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction goes forward; Q(0.30) = 0.396 > K, so ΔG > 0 and it goes backward. At equilibrium ξ = 0.2293 mol, conversion of A = 0.229 (22.9%), and yield of B = 0.459 mol B per mol A fed.
examples.check:
import math
K = 0.222
def Q(xi):
    return 4.0*xi**2/(1.0 - xi**2)
q1 = Q(0.10)
q2 = Q(0.30)
xi_eq = math.sqrt(K/(4.0 + K))
X = xi_eq/1.0
yB = 2.0*xi_eq/1.0
print(round(q1, 4))
print(round(q2, 3))
print(round(xi_eq, 4))
print(round(X, 3))
print(round(yB, 3))

traps: Reporting K > 1 as high conversion. K fixes only the equilibrium activity ratio; stoichiometry, feed, pressure and inerts also matter.
Using ΔG° sign for feasibility at the plant composition. Feasibility uses ΔG = RT ln(Q/K), not ΔG° alone.

Treating Q as if it were K. Q can be evaluated at any composition and it changes as the reaction proceeds; only at equilibrium does Q equal K. K is the fixed value of Q at equilibrium for the given temperature.
Confusing yield with selectivity. Yield is desired product per limiting reactant fed; selectivity is desired product per undesired product.
Forgetting pressure in gas activities. aᵢ = yᵢP/P° for an ideal gas; yᵢ alone is correct only when P = P° = 1 bar.

quiz.q: Write the reaction quotient for a single reaction.
quiz.a: Q = Π aᵢ<sup>νᵢ</sup>, product over species; νᵢ is positive for products and negative for reactants; aᵢ are activities at the current composition.

quiz.q: Why does K > 1 not guarantee high equilibrium conversion?
quiz.a: K fixes only the equilibrium activity ratio. Conversion also depends on stoichiometry, feed composition, pressure and inerts; a large product coefficient or dilute feed can keep conversion low.

quiz.q: For A ⇌ 2B at 1 bar, 1 mol A fed, K = 0.222 at 400 K. Find Q at ξ = 0.20 mol and state the direction.
quiz.a: Q = 4(0.20)²/(1 − 0.20²) = 0.1667. Q < K, so ΔG < 0 and the reaction goes forward.

quiz.q: Same system: find equilibrium conversion of A.
A mixture of A and B has Q > K for A ⇌ 2B. Which way does it move, and what happens to Q?
quiz.a: It moves backward, B → A. For this stoichiometry Q = 4ξ²/(1 − ξ²) increases with ξ; backward reaction lowers ξ and lowers Q until Q = K.

quiz.q: A reactor has high selectivity to D but low yield of D. Explain.
quiz.a: Selectivity compares D with undesired product; yield compares D formed with limiting reactant fed. High selectivity with low conversion means little feed reacted, so little D formed.

quiz.q: If Q = 0.5K, what is the sign of ΔG and the direction?
quiz.a: ΔG = RT ln(0.5) < 0, so the forward reaction is spontaneous.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant design uses the same Q-versus-K test inside flowsheet software, where Gibbs energy minimisation handles many reactions and phases at once. Ammonia and methanol synthesis, steam reforming and biorefinery routes are screened this way before reactor sizing. Research extends the idea to electrolyte and solid-phase reactions by changing activity definitions. Search next for reaction quotient, equilibrium conversion, selectivity and Gibbs energy minimisation.
